title: US Revokes Citizenship of Indian-Born Cab Driver Convicted of Rape and Kidnapping
excerpt: A federal court has stripped Gurmeet Singh of his U.S. citizenship after he concealed a violent sexual assault during the naturalization process, in a case that is part of the Justice Department's broader denaturalization push.
body:
• A U.S. federal court revoked the citizenship of Gurmeet Singh, an India-born cab driver convicted of first-degree rape and kidnapping in New York.
  • Singh concealed the violent assault from immigration authorities during his naturalization process in 2011, weeks after the crime.
  • He is serving a 20-year prison sentence and faces potential deportation upon release in 2029.
  • The case is part of the Justice Department's expanded denaturalization campaign targeting individuals who obtained citizenship through fraud.

Federal Court Strips Citizenship

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York has revoked the citizenship of Gurmeet Singh, a 55-year-old India-born man convicted of raping and kidnapping a female passenger while working as a taxicab driver in New York City, the Justice Department announced.

The Aug. 26 order follows a civil denaturalization complaint the Justice Department filed on Feb. 2, alleging that Singh concealed the violent crime throughout his naturalization proceedings. Singh became a U.S. citizen on Oct. 19, 2011 — just months after committing the assault.

"American citizenship is not a shield for criminals. Gurmeet Singh, a convicted rapist from India, is no longer a U.S. citizen."

— Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney General

The Crime and Concealment

According to the Justice Department, Singh was driving his taxi in May 2011 when he picked up a female passenger who fell asleep during the ride home to the East Village. Instead of delivering her to her destination, Singh drove to an isolated location.

When the passenger awoke, she found Singh on top of her with a knife against her throat. He threatened her, bound and gagged her, blindfolded her, removed her clothes and raped her, according to court documents. The victim escaped at dawn and flagged down a passerby for help.

Weeks after the assault, Singh filed his application for U.S. citizenship. He did not disclose the crime on his naturalization application and became a citizen that October. He was subsequently convicted in 2014 of Rape in the First Degree and Kidnapping in the Second Degree as a Sexually Motivated Felony, and was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Part of Broader Denaturalization Push

The case falls within the Justice Department's expanded denaturalization initiative, which targets naturalized citizens who concealed serious crimes, war crimes or fraud during the citizenship process. According to the Washington Times, federal prosecutors are now pursuing violent criminals, gun offenders, human traffickers and fraudsters across the country.

Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said Singh had "unlawfully obtained the privileges of U.S. citizenship by concealing horrible criminal acts" and pledged the Department would "continue to protect the integrity of the citizenship process."

U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York said the ruling "sends a strong message to those who obtain citizenship through deceit."

Immigration History

Singh first entered the United States in February 1992 as a temporary visitor authorized to stay for six months. He overstayed his visa and remained in the country without authorization for years until a family-based immigrant visa petition allowed him to become a permanent resident in June 2000, according to the Justice Department.

He is currently incarcerated at Shawangunk Correctional Facility, a maximum-security prison in Wallkill, New York, which also houses serial killer David Berkowitz. Singh is currently set to be released in February 2029.

What Happens Next

With his citizenship revoked, Singh is required to surrender all documentation of his former U.S. citizenship. Upon his release from prison, the Department of Homeland Security will determine whether to initiate deportation proceedings. The case was prosecuted by Trial Attorney Christopher Lyerla of the Civil Division's Office of Immigration Litigation and Assistant U.S. Attorney Layaliza Soloveichik.
nri_angle: The case underscores how the U.S. government's expanded denaturalization campaign can revoke citizenship from naturalized immigrants, including those from India, who concealed criminal conduct.
